answers.answer: Replication copies data changes between servers; each maintained copy is a replica. It keeps the same data in several places, whereas partitioning/sharding divides data into groups; each group can itself have replicas. Copies can serve more reads or take over after a failure, but read routing and safe takeover need separate setup, lag can produce old reads, and copying writes does not automatically increase write capacity. A new replica starts with a snapshot at a known point and receives later change-log records. The log records source changes; applying them updates replica data so queries can see it. The snapshot and starting log position must agree to avoid missing or incorrectly applying changes, and dependent changes need source order. Received records may still be unapplied, so receipt does not establish visibility.

evidence.quote: Copies data changes between servers. Each maintained copy is a replica.
Read routing and a safe takeover process are separate design work; a second copy does not configure either automatically.
The initial copy and starting log position must agree. Otherwise the handoff can miss changes or apply them incorrectly.
The replica updated its data so queries can see the change.

answers.answer: Asynchronous replication lets the writing server acknowledge before a replica confirms the change; acknowledgement means only the configured success condition was met. If the primary acknowledges, permanently fails before sending the change, and that replica is promoted, the replacement lacks the confirmed write. Avoiding the replica wait reduces write delay; acknowledgement alone proves no second copy. Synchronous replication waits for required replicas before success. Specify their set or count and whether confirmation means received (possibly memory only), stored durably (survives restart), or applied (query-visible). Waiting for durable copies protects against loss of the writer but adds delay and can stall writes when too few required replicas respond. Async avoids that acknowledgement dependency but risks stale reads and recent-write loss. Synchronous success need not involve every replica or ensure every read is current. It does not protect against losing all copies or accidental logical changes.

evidence.quote: The writing server can acknowledge success before a replica confirms the change. Acknowledgement means the configured success condition was met, not that every copy has the data.
If the writing server fails permanently before sending a confirmed change, a replacement replica will not have that change.
Choose the required replica set or count and acknowledgement stage.
Waiting for durable copies protects against losing the writing server. It adds delay, and writes can stall if too few required replicas respond.

answers.answer: Replication lag means a copy is behind in receiving or applying source changes. A successful write can therefore be followed by an old replica value, including when the record has arrived but is unapplied. Read-your-writes means later reads include your completed change or newer state. Reading from the still-authoritative primary avoids waiting for a replica but concentrates load and requires correct authority after failover. Waiting for proof that a chosen replica applied this specific write adds delay and can fail. Fixed sleeps and low average lag are insufficient. Accepting stale reads suits delay-tolerant work and avoids a freshness wait, but cannot promise the completed change is visible. Routing cannot recover a write lost during failover. A leader accepts writes: single leader gives one server responsibility and one ordering place for a dataset, with followers copying and failover needed for replacement. Multiple leaders accept and exchange writes, potentially nearer users, but independent edits require conflict rules; timestamp choice may discard a valid edit. Leaderless requests use any coordinator to contact the relevant replicas, wait for a configured reply count, repair differences and reconcile concurrent versions. More write entry points do not ensure conflict freedom or one current value; topology alone also does not determine synchronous versus asynchronous behavior.

evidence.quote: A replica is behind the source in receiving or applying changes. State which stage a lag measurement describes; data received but not applied is not yet visible to reads.
Primary reads concentrate load and require correct authority after failover. Waiting for a replica adds delay and can fail. Routing alone cannot recover a write already lost during failover.
One server accepts writes for a set of data. Followers copy its changes.
Concurrent versions still need reconciliation; no topology name guarantees one current value or conflict-free updates.

answers.answer: Failover transfers a failed server's responsibilities. In single-leader replication, promotion makes a suitable replica the new leader and routing redirects application connections to it. A silent leader may merely have a broken network connection while still accepting writes. Split brain is two servers acting as sole leader and accepting potentially conflicting changes. Choose a sufficiently current suitable replica to preserve recent writes, fence the old leader by shutdown or blocked access so it cannot keep writing, and redirect clients to the replacement. The lesson does not specify a concrete eligibility test or automated fencing protocol. Acknowledged asynchronous writes absent from the replica can be lost. A healthy current replica may have faithfully applied an accidental deletion, so it cannot necessarily supply the earlier data. A backup preserves earlier recoverable state; point-in-time recovery restores a backup and replays saved logs to a selected time before deletion. Retention and available logs bound history. Restore tests must reconstruct usable application data and measure recovery duration; mere backup-file existence or a current replica alone proves neither recovery time nor historical recoverability.

evidence.quote: Moves a failed server's responsibilities to another server. In a single-leader system, the process selects a suitable replica, promotes it to leader, and redirects application connections.
A missing response does not prove the old leader stopped. Its network connection can be broken while it still accepts writes.
Prevents the old leader from continuing to write, for example by shutting it down or blocking its access.
Retention and available logs bound recoverable history. Restore tests must reconstruct usable application data and measure how long recovery takes; file existence alone proves neither.

answers.answer: First establish acceptable loss of acknowledged writes, reporting staleness, maximum write delay and recovery downtime. Use a single writing leader with replicas and require durable replica acknowledgement from a specified set/count chosen for the server failures to be survived; the lesson supplies no numeric requirement or concrete selection procedure, so I cannot fix the count from this scenario alone. This reduces loss risk if the writer fails, while adding commit delay and potentially stalling writes if the required replicas are unavailable. Route delay-tolerant reporting to replicas within the agreed freshness allowance; freshness-sensitive reads use the authoritative primary or proof of application of the relevant write. Prepare takeover by selecting a suitable current replica, fencing the previous leader and redirecting clients; test it against the downtime and loss targets. Preserve backups and enough logs for the required historical window, and test restoration to usable data, including recovery duration. Monitor replication progress, lag with its receiving/applying stage specified, health, write waits and commit delay. Replication alone cannot promise zero loss or uninterrupted writes: acknowledgements have different meanings, async can lose recent confirmed writes, all copies can be lost or replicate unwanted changes, and agreement-dependent writes must wait or fail during a network split. Independent writes require handling stale reads and conflicts.

evidence.quote: Choose acceptable acknowledged-write loss, read freshness, write latency and recovery time before choosing replica settings.

Delay-tolerant reads can use replicas. Freshness-sensitive reads need suitable routing or progress checks. Waiting for durable replica acknowledgements narrows some loss windows but adds commit delay and dependence on those replicas.
Copies consume storage, network and operating work. Monitor replication progress, lag, health and write waits; exercise failover and historical restore against the required recovery targets.
During a network split, operations that need agreement with unreachable copies must wait or fail.
